# Worked example — Vercel Sandbox

Load this when writing the base-snapshot, auth, or `create` script for a snapshot-capable cloud
provider. It fills section 7's skeletons with a real surface, `vercel sandbox
create|exec|snapshot|remove`. Adapt the names and verify every flag against
`vercel sandbox --help` for the user's CLI version.

This is the Orca-server connection mode: the recipe emits a pairing URL. If the user chose SSH in
the interview, use `references/ssh-host.md` instead.

## Snapshot cleanup

The base and auth excerpts each belong to one `set -euo pipefail` script. Include this function
in both scripts and arm the trap before creating their temporary sandbox. Keep it armed through
verification, snapshot creation, and writing state; cleanup failure must remain visible.

Use the guarded array expansion below so an empty `vercel_args` array works under `set -u`
on stock macOS Bash 3.2 while preserving each configured argument.

```bash
cleanup_snapshot() {
  snapshot_exit=$?
  trap - EXIT
  if ! vercel sandbox remove "$1" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} >&2; then
    echo "Sandbox cleanup failed for $1; inspect and remove it before continuing" >&2
    snapshot_exit=1
  fi
  exit "$snapshot_exit"
}
```

Use fresh sandbox names for these scripts so cleanup cannot remove an existing environment.

## Base snapshot

Provision, install tools and clone, build headless, then snapshot.

```bash
# provision a fresh build sandbox (retain a couple of snapshots)
trap 'cleanup_snapshot "$base"' EXIT
vercel sandbox create --name "$base" --runtime node24 --timeout 30m --vcpus 4 --publish-port "$port" \
  --snapshot-expiration 30d --keep-last-snapshots 2 ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} >&2
# remote build (long timeout): install pkgs+gh+pnpm+agent CLI, clone with GIT_ASKPASS (the helper's
# \$1/\$GH_TOKEN escaping is load-bearing — see the guide's Credentials section — then
# `rm -f /tmp/askpass.sh`), write the headless main-only build config (drop the renderer), dev setup,
# build CLI + headless main, smoke-check
vercel sandbox exec "$base" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} --timeout 25m --env "GH_TOKEN=$gh_token" … -- bash -lc '…build…' >&2
# snapshot the STOPPED sandbox and parse the id from CLI output (fail if unparseable)
out="$(vercel sandbox snapshot "$base" --stop --expiration 30d ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} 2>&1)"; printf '%s\n' "$out" >&2
snapshot_id="$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -nE 's/.*(snap_[A-Za-z0-9]+).*/\1/p' | tail -1)"
[ -n "$snapshot_id" ] || { echo "snapshot id missing" >&2; exit 1; }
# merge { baseName, snapshotId, scope, project, port, repoUrl, repoRef, projectRoot } into state; print state JSON
```

## Agent-auth snapshot

Boot the base, let the user log the agent in, verify, then re-snapshot. `codex` here is an example;
substitute the user's chosen agent's login and status verbs.

```bash
trap 'cleanup_snapshot "$auth"' EXIT
vercel sandbox create --name "$auth" --snapshot "$snapshot_id" --timeout 30m --publish-port "$port" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} >&2
# The USER runs this in their own terminal and completes the URL/code on the HOST.
vercel sandbox exec --interactive --tty "$auth" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} -- bash -lc 'codex login --device-auth'
```

Verify by exit code. The remote command prints a sentinel instead of relying on the exit code,
because a provider CLI may not propagate remote exit codes:

```bash
verdict="$(vercel sandbox exec "$auth" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} --timeout 30s \
  -- bash -lc 'if codex login status >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo ORCA_AGENT_LOGGED_IN; else echo ORCA_AGENT_LOGGED_OUT; fi')"
case "$verdict" in
  *ORCA_AGENT_LOGGED_IN*) ;;
  *) echo "agent not logged in; not snapshotting" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
```

Fallback for an agent whose `status` exit code says nothing about auth: capture the output with
stderr folded in and match the agent's exact success line. Match a variable, not a pipe, so the
provider process cannot take SIGPIPE:

```bash
status="$(vercel sandbox exec "$auth" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} --timeout 30s -- bash -lc 'codex login status 2>&1')"
grep -Eq 'Logged in using ChatGPT|Logged in via device' <<<"$status" \
  || { echo "agent not logged in; not snapshotting" >&2; exit 1; }
```

Then re-snapshot and record the new id:

```bash
out="$(vercel sandbox snapshot "$auth" --stop --expiration 30d ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} 2>&1)"; printf '%s\n' "$out" >&2
new_id="$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -nE 's/.*(snap_[A-Za-z0-9]+).*/\1/p' | tail -1)"
[ -n "$new_id" ] || { echo "authenticated snapshot id missing" >&2; exit 1; }
# overwrite state.snapshotId = new_id, record authSourceSnapshotId = snapshot_id; remove the auth sandbox
```

## Per-workspace `create`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# resolve from env→state→fallback: snapshot_id, scope, project, port, repo_url, repo_ref, project_root
vercel_args=(); [ -n "$scope" ] && vercel_args+=(--scope "$scope"); [ -n "$project" ] && vercel_args+=(--project "$project")
[ -n "$snapshot_id" ] || { echo "snapshotId missing — build the base and auth snapshots first" >&2; exit 1; }
gh_token="[REDACTED] -v gh >/dev/null 2>&1 && gh auth token 2>/dev/null || true)}}"
recipe_id="${ORCA_RECIPE_ID:-vercel-sandbox}"
recipe_id="${recipe_id//./-}"  # Vercel names forbid dots.
instance_id="${ORCA_VM_INSTANCE_ID:-$(date +%s)}"
max_recipe_id_length=$((128 - ${#instance_id} - 6))  # Preserve the unique instance suffix.
[ "$max_recipe_id_length" -gt 0 ] || { echo "ORCA_VM_INSTANCE_ID is too long for a Vercel sandbox name" >&2; exit 1; }
name="orca-${recipe_id:0:max_recipe_id_length}-${instance_id}"

# Arm cleanup BEFORE create so a failing create can't leak a half-built paid sandbox.
cleanup_on_error() { [ "$?" -ne 0 ] && vercel sandbox remove "$name" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; }
trap cleanup_on_error EXIT

# 1. boot from the authenticated snapshot, publish the serve port
create_output="$(vercel sandbox create --name "$name" --snapshot "$snapshot_id" \
  --timeout 30m --publish-port "$port" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} 2>&1)"; printf '%s\n' "$create_output" >&2
# Vercel prints the published https URL; derive the external wss:// pairing address from it
public_url="$(printf '%s\n' "$create_output" | sed -nE 's#.*(https://[^[:space:]]+\.vercel\.run).*#\1#p' | head -1)"
[ -n "$public_url" ] || { echo "no published URL in create output" >&2; exit 1; }
pairing_ws="${public_url/https:\/\//wss://}"

# 2. (remote) ensure the repo is at the right commit; rebuild only if the commit changed (cache marker)
vercel sandbox exec "$name" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} --timeout 20m \
  --env "GH_TOKEN=$gh_token" --env "ORCA_PROJECT_ROOT=$project_root" \
  --env "ORCA_REPO_URL=$repo_url" --env "ORCA_REPO_REF=$repo_ref" \
  -- bash -lc 'set -euo pipefail; cd "$ORCA_PROJECT_ROOT"; \
    export GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0; \
    # Escaping is load-bearing here: re-test the fetch after any edit to the nested quoting.
    if [ -n "${GH_TOKEN:-}" ]; then \
      printf "%s\n" "#!/usr/bin/env bash" "case \"\$1\" in *Username*) echo x-access-token;; *Password*) echo \"\$GH_TOKEN\";; esac" > /tmp/askpass.sh; \
      chmod 700 /tmp/askpass.sh; export GIT_ASKPASS=/tmp/askpass.sh; fi; \
    git fetch origin "$ORCA_REPO_REF"; \
    git checkout -B "$ORCA_REPO_REF" FETCH_HEAD; \
    rm -f /tmp/askpass.sh; \
    c="$(git rev-parse HEAD)"; [ -f .orca-built ] && [ "$(cat .orca-built)" = "$c" ] || { \
      pnpm install --prefer-offline && pnpm run build:cli && \
      node config/scripts/desktop-build/execution/run-electron-vite-build.mjs --config config/electron-vite.vm-serve.config.ts && \
      printf "%s" "$c" > .orca-built; }' >&2

# 3. (remote) start orca serve in the background, writing recipe JSON to a file; poll until it parses
recipe_json="$(vercel sandbox exec "$name" ${vercel_args[@]+"${vercel_args[@]}"} --timeout 60s \
  --env "ORCA_PORT=$port" --env "ORCA_PROJECT_ROOT=$project_root" --env "ORCA_PAIRING_ADDRESS=$pairing_ws" \
  -- bash -lc 'set -euo pipefail; cd "$ORCA_PROJECT_ROOT"; rm -f /tmp/orca-recipe.json /tmp/orca-serve.log; \
    nohup pnpm exec orca-dev serve --port "$ORCA_PORT" --project-root "$ORCA_PROJECT_ROOT" \
      --pairing-address "$ORCA_PAIRING_ADDRESS" --recipe-json >/tmp/orca-recipe.json 2>/tmp/orca-serve.log </dev/null & \
    pid=$!; for _ in $(seq 1 80); do \
      node -e "JSON.parse(require(\"node:fs\").readFileSync(\"/tmp/orca-recipe.json\",\"utf8\"))" >/dev/null 2>&1 && { cat /tmp/orca-recipe.json; exit 0; }; \
      kill -0 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || { cat /tmp/orca-serve.log >&2; exit 1; }; sleep 0.25; \
    done; cat /tmp/orca-serve.log >&2; echo "serve recipe JSON timed out" >&2; exit 1')"

# 4. print serve's JSON enriched with userData (single object on stdout)
node -e 'const p=JSON.parse(process.argv[1]); console.log(JSON.stringify({...p, schemaVersion:1,
  userData:{...p.userData, provider:"vercel-sandbox", resourceId:process.argv[2], snapshotId:process.argv[3]}}))' \
  "$recipe_json" "$name" "$snapshot_id"
trap - EXIT
```

`suspend`, `resume`, and `destroy` run `vercel sandbox stop|...|remove "$resource_id"`, reading
`userData.resourceId` from the lifecycle payload on stdin.

The `128` in `max_recipe_id_length` is Vercel's sandbox name cap. Confirm it against
`vercel sandbox create --help` or Vercel's docs for the user's CLI version before relying on it; a
wrong cap silently truncates recipe ids in resource names.

# Host API by surface

<!-- Generated by config/scripts/generate-plugin-authoring-skill-references.mjs. Do not edit. -->

Host API 1.10 (`"pluginApi": 1`). Call `host.call(method, params, { signal })`; a surface not listed for a method gets `not_permitted`. Params are strict: a field this Orca does not know is refused with `invalid_params`, so check `host.has(method)` or `api.minor` before using a method newer than your `engines.orca` floor. Each call also needs the manifest capability and the user's approval.

## Methods per surface

- Worker (`trusted-worker`, `main`): `orca` passed to `activate(orca)`: `workspace.readContext`, `terminal.sendText`, `notifications.show`, `storage.get`, `storage.set`, `storage.delete`, `storage.keys`, `secrets.get`, `secrets.set`, `secrets.delete`, `secrets.protection`, `settings.get`, `settings.set`, `agents.list`, `statusBar.update`, `appearance.read`, `appearance.apply`, `workspace.list`, `project.list`, `workspace.open`, `workspace.rename`, `terminal.create`, `terminal.read`, `agent.launch`, `editor.open`, `commands.run`, `project.setHidden`, `terminal.list`, `terminal.focus`, `terminal.close`, `workspace.create`, `agent.resume`, `automation.list`, `automation.create`, `automation.update`, `automation.delete`, `agent.listSessions`, `editor.readTypography`
- Panel: global `orca` in an HTML panel; `host` imported from `orca` in a components panel: `workspace.readContext`, `notifications.show`, `storage.get`, `storage.set`, `storage.delete`, `storage.keys`, `secrets.get`, `secrets.set`, `secrets.delete`, `secrets.protection`, `settings.get`, `settings.set`, `shell.openExternal`, `files.saveAs`, `plugin.request`, `agents.list`, `events.subscribe`, `editor.readTypography`
- Custom editor: global `orca` in the editor frame: `workspace.readContext`, `notifications.show`, `storage.get`, `storage.set`, `storage.delete`, `storage.keys`, `secrets.get`, `secrets.set`, `secrets.delete`, `secrets.protection`, `settings.get`, `settings.set`, `shell.openExternal`, `files.saveAs`, `plugin.request`, `agents.list`, `events.subscribe`, `editor.readTypography`

## Worker API (`import type { OrcaWorkerApi } from 'orca/worker'`)

- `api: HostApiVersion`
- `commands.register(commandId: string, handler: (args: unknown, context: CommandContext) => unknown)`: A string result is shown as-is in Orca; anything else as JSON.
- `events.on(event: E, handler: (payload: PluginEvents[E]) => void | Promise<void>)`: Only events listed in the manifest's `contributes.events` arrive.
- `hooks.on(hook: H, handler: HookHandler<H>)`: Only hooks listed in `contributes.hooks` run. Return `next(event)` to go on (with the fields the hook allows changed), a result such as `{ deny: reason }` to stop, or nothing to pass. Plugins run in turn, then Orca acts; past 2 s, or on a throw, Orca carries on as if this plugin passed and logs it.
- `host: HostApi<'worker'>`
- `panels: PanelsApi`: This plugin's panels and custom editors.
- `storage: StorageApi`: Same store as panels' `storage` (`storage:own`); `onDidChange` hears their writes too.
- `settings: SettingsApi`: `settings:own`; `onDidChange` also hears the person changing them in Settings.
- `secrets: SecretsApi`: `secrets:own`.
- `grantedCapabilities: readonly string[]`: Consented capability kinds; informational, the host re-checks every call.
- `log(message: string)`: Lands in `orca plugin logs`.

## Frame API (global `orca`, also `window.orca`, in HTML panels and custom editors)

- `api: HostApiVersion`
- `host: HostApi<'panel' | 'editor'>`
- `on(event: E, handler: (payload: FrameEvents[E]) => unknown)`
- `locale: string`: Orca's UI language as a BCP-47 tag.
- `plugin: PluginBridgeApi`: Your plugin's own worker: `request` its handlers, hear what it `post`s.
- `storage: StorageApi`: The plugin's own storage, the same its worker uses (`storage:own`).
- `settings: SettingsApi`: The plugin's settings, declared ones with their defaults (`settings:own`).
- `secrets: SecretsApi`: The plugin's encrypted secrets (`secrets:own`).
- `shell.openExternal(url: string)`: `reason`: the person cancelled, or Orca's window was hidden so nobody could confirm.
- `files.saveAs(options: SaveAsOptions)`: Desktop isolated frames only; `cancelled` when the person closes the dialog.
- `document?: EditorDocumentApi`: Custom editors only. Orca keeps no undo history for them: Cmd/Ctrl+Z reaches the frame.
- `document.get()`: The latest document, with your accepted edits' content at the same version.
- `document.onDidChange(handler: (document: EditorDocument) => void)`: Replays the current document, then each one Orca sends when the file changes outside.
- `document.applyEdit(edit: EditorEdit)`: Rejects with `conflict`, `too_large` or `not_permitted` (read-only).
- `document.session(options?: EditorSessionOptions<T>)`: Document sync in one call; resolves once theme, locale and the first document are in.

## Theme variables in frames

HTML panels and custom editors get these CSS variables from Orca's active theme and fonts, plus a `light` or `dark` class on `<html>`. A theme or font change updates them in place and emits `theme` (`orca.on('theme', ...)`); the frame is not reloaded. Style from them, not fixed colours.

- `--orca-background`: App canvas
- `--orca-foreground`: Body text
- `--orca-card`: Cards and panels
- `--orca-card-foreground`: Text on `--orca-card`
- `--orca-popover`: Menus, popovers and dialogs
- `--orca-popover-foreground`: Text on `--orca-popover`
- `--orca-primary`: Primary buttons
- `--orca-primary-foreground`: Text on `--orca-primary`
- `--orca-secondary`: Secondary buttons
- `--orca-secondary-foreground`: Text on `--orca-secondary`
- `--orca-muted`: Quiet fills
- `--orca-muted-foreground`: Secondary text
- `--orca-accent`: Hover and selected fills
- `--orca-accent-foreground`: Text on `--orca-accent`
- `--orca-destructive`
- `--orca-destructive-foreground`
- `--orca-border`: Borders and separators
- `--orca-input`: Input borders
- `--orca-ring`: Focus rings
- `--orca-radius`: Corner radius of cards and controls
- `--orca-font-sans`: Interface font stack. Fonts Orca loads itself (the default Geist, plugin fonts) are not in frames, so the next installed font in the stack is used
- `--orca-font-mono`: Monospace font stack for code

## Methods

- `workspace.readContext` (capability `workspace:read`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Id, branch, name and terminal ids of the focused workspace, or null when none is focused.
  `(params?: {}) => { workspaceId?: string; branch: string; displayName: string; terminals: { id: string; title?: string }[] } | null`
- `terminal.sendText` (capability `terminal:send`; worker; since 1.0): Types text into one terminal named by id, optionally pressing Enter.
  `(params: { terminalId: string; text: string; enter?: boolean }) => { accepted: boolean }`
- `notifications.show` (capability `notifications:show`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Shows a desktop notification.
  `(params: { title: string; body?: string }) => { delivered: boolean }`
- `storage.get` (capability `storage:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Reads a JSON value from the plugin's private store; null when absent.
  `(params: { key: string }) => { value: JSON }`
- `storage.set` (capability `storage:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Writes a JSON value to the plugin's private store.
  `(params: { key: string; value: JSON }) => { ok: true }`
- `storage.delete` (capability `storage:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Removes a key from the plugin's private store.
  `(params: { key: string }) => { ok: true }`
- `storage.keys` (capability `storage:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Lists the keys in the plugin's private store.
  `(params?: {}) => { keys: string[] }`
- `secrets.get` (capability `secrets:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Reads a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file; null when absent.
  `(params: { key: string }) => { value: string | null }`
- `secrets.set` (capability `secrets:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Stores a secret in the plugin's encrypted secrets file.
  `(params: { key: string; value: string }) => { ok: true }`
- `secrets.delete` (capability `secrets:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Removes a secret from the plugin's encrypted secrets file.
  `(params: { key: string }) => { ok: true }`
- `secrets.protection` (capability `secrets:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.1): How secrets are protected at rest: `os-keyring`, or `unavailable` (no OS key store, or Linux `basic_text`), where `secrets.set` fails.
  `(params?: {}) => { status: "os-keyring" | "unavailable" }`
- `settings.get` (capability `settings:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Reads every setting the plugin owns.
  `(params?: {}) => { settings: Record<string, JSON> }`
- `settings.set` (capability `settings:own`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.0): Writes one setting the plugin owns.
  `(params: { key: string; value: JSON }) => { ok: true }`
- `shell.openExternal` (no capability; panel, editor; since 1.1; needs a user gesture): Opens an http:, https: or mailto: URL in the default browser. Needs a click or key press in the frame; desktop app only. Orca asks the person before an http(s) host the plugin was not allowed; `opened` is false if they cancel.
  `(params: { url: string }) => { opened: boolean; reason?: "cancelled" | "consent-unavailable" }`
- `files.saveAs` (no capability; panel, editor; since 1.1; needs a user gesture): Offers data (a string or ArrayBuffer, up to 64 MiB) in Orca's save dialog; the plugin never learns the path. Needs a click or key press in the frame; desktop app only.
  `(params: { suggestedName?: string; mimeType?: string; data: string | ArrayBuffer }) => { status: "saved" | "cancelled" }`
- `plugin.request` (no capability; panel, editor; since 1.2): Asks the plugin's own worker to run the handler it registered with `orca.panels.handle(name)`, starting the worker if needed; resolves with what the handler returned. `unknown_method` when no handler has that name.
  `(params: { name: string; input?: JSON; timeoutMs?: number }) => { output: JSON }`
- `agents.list` (capability `agent:read`; worker, panel, editor; since 1.2): The agents in the focused workspace, or in the one `workspaceId` names (rejected when no workspace has it): their terminal, title, agent kind, status, session and dispatched task. `agent.status.changed` reports each change after.
  `(params?: { workspaceId?: string }) => { agents: { terminalId: string | null; title: string | null; agent: string | null; state: "working" | "blocked" | "waiting" | "done"; stateStartedAt: number; sessionId?: string | null; task?: { title: string } | null }[] }`
- `events.subscribe` (no capability; panel, editor; since 1.2): Delivers a workspace, agent or editor event to this panel as `orca.on(event)`; needs the event's read capability, when it has one. The frame APIs call it for you.
  `(params: { event: "workspace.created" | "workspace.removed" | "agent.status.changed" | "workspace.changed" | "editor.typography.changed" }) => { ok: true }`
- `statusBar.update` (no capability; worker; since 1.2): Changes one of the plugin's `contributes.statusBarItems` (named by `id`): fields given replace their current value, `visible: false` hides it. Desktop app only; lasts until Orca restarts, and is hidden while the plugin is disabled. A plugin with `main` and status bar items has its worker started when it is enabled and kept running while it stays enabled, so a worker can poll and update its items without an event or a hook.
  `(params: { id: string; text?: string; icon?: "activity" | "bar-chart-3" | "bell" | "blocks" | "book" | "bot" | "bug" | "calendar" | "cloud" | "code" | "database" | "file-text" | "flag" | "folder" | "gauge" | "globe" | "hammer" | "layers" | "lightbulb" | "package" | "plug" | "puzzle" | "rocket" | "star" | "terminal" | "wrench" | "zap" | "add" | "remove" | "delete" | "edit" | "refresh" | "search" | "settings" | "check" | "close" | "info" | "warning" | "error" | "open-external" | "copy" | "download" | "upload" | "play" | "pause" | "stop" | "more" | "expand" | "collapse" | "next" | "filter" | "branch" | "file" | "agent" | "link"; tone?: "neutral" | "accent" | "success" | "warning" | "danger"; tooltip?: string; visible?: boolean }) => { ok: true }`
- `appearance.read` (capability `appearance:write`; worker; since 1.4): Reads the current desktop appearance revision for a conditional update.
  `(params?: {}) => { revision: string }`
- `appearance.apply` (capability `appearance:write`; worker; since 1.4): Publishes owned app/editor and terminal colors and selects them in the desktop. Returns publication, not renderer acknowledgement.
  `(params: { expectedRevision: string; app: string; terminal: string }) => { revision: string; themeId: string; mode: "dark" | "light"; delivery: "published" }`
- `workspace.list` (capability `workspace:read`; worker; since 1.3): Lists every workspace, Git worktrees and folders, on every host Orca reaches; `includeStatus` (host API 1.7) adds each one's agent status. `hostId` is the host a row records (`local`, `ssh:…`, `runtime:…`), or null when it records none, as for a project-group folder on this machine.
  `(params?: { includeStatus?: boolean }) => { workspaces: { id: string; kind: "worktree" | "folder"; name: string; project?: string | null; projectId?: string | null; path: string; branch: string | null; hostId: string | null; status?: { state: "working" | "permission" | "done" | "active" | "inactive"; unread: boolean; terminalCount: number; lastActivityAt: number | null } }[]; truncated: boolean; statusTruncated?: boolean }`
- `project.list` (capability `workspace:read`; worker; since 1.7): Lists your projects (repositories and folders) on every host; `id` is what `workspace.list` rows name as `projectId`. `hostId` is always named: `local`, `ssh:…` or `runtime:…`.
  `(params?: {}) => { projects: { id: string; name: string; kind: "git" | "folder"; hostId: string | null; path: string; hidden?: boolean }[]; truncated: boolean }`
- `workspace.open` (capability `workspace:write`; worker; since 1.3): Shows a workspace in Orca, as clicking it in the sidebar does; a folder workspace needs the desktop app.
  `(params: { workspaceId: string }) => { opened: true }`
- `workspace.rename` (capability `workspace:write`; worker; since 1.5): Renames a workspace in Orca's sidebar, as renaming it by hand does; the name stays until it is renamed again.
  `(params: { workspaceId: string; name: string }) => { name: string }`
- `terminal.create` (capability `terminal:send`; worker; since 1.3): Opens a terminal in a workspace, optionally running a command, in the background.
  `(params: { workspaceId: string; title?: string; command?: string }) => { terminalId: string }`
- `terminal.read` (capability `terminal:read`; worker; since 1.3): Reads a terminal's newest output as plain text, at most 2000 lines.
  `(params: { terminalId: string; maxLines?: number }) => { lines: string[]; truncated: boolean }`
- `agent.launch` (capability `agent:launch`; worker; since 1.3): Starts an agent's CLI in a new terminal of a workspace, in the background, and returns as soon as it starts; a `prompt` is sent once the agent is ready.
  `(params: { workspaceId: string; agent: string; prompt?: string }) => { terminalId: string }`

## Hooks

List each in `contributes.hooks` (`{ "event", "onError"? }`; `main` and `trusted-worker`) and handle it with `orca.hooks.on(event, (event, next) => ...)`. Return `next(event)` (or nothing) to go on, or the stop result. Plugins run in turn, 2 s each; a throw, timeout or crash passes unless the entry says `"onError": "deny"`. Decide first: an awaited call before you return (a notification, say) can fail or time out and turn your deny into a pass.

- `terminal.send` (since 1.4.248): Text Orca, the CLI or a plugin is about to send to a terminal. A person typing (on the desktop, a phone or a paired client) is never hooked, and prompts Orca submits to an agent take `agent.prompt.before` instead. Writes to one terminal stay in order while a hook decides. Rewrite `text` or `enter` with `next`, or return `{ deny }` to refuse the send.
  event `{ terminalId: string; text: string; enter: boolean; inputKind: "driving" | "orchestration" | "launch" }`; `next` may change `text`, `enter`; stop with `{ deny: string }`
- `workspace.create.before` (since 1.4.248): A worktree or folder workspace is about to be created. Change `name`, `branch` or `base` with `next`, or return `{ deny }` to refuse it.
  event `{ kind: "worktree" | "folder"; projectId: string; name: string; branch?: string; base?: string }`; `next` may change `name`, `branch`, `base`; stop with `{ deny: string }`
- `workspace.create.after` (since 1.4.248): A worktree or folder workspace was created. Observe only: Orca does not wait for it, and results are ignored.
  event `{ workspaceId: string; kind: "worktree" | "folder"; path: string; branch: string }`; `next` may change nothing; stop with nothing (observe only)
- `agent.launch.before` (since 1.4.248): Orca is about to start an agent CLI in a terminal, from any launcher (new tab, workspace create, CLI, automation, orchestration). Change `command` or add `env` with `next`, or return `{ deny }` to refuse the launch. Restores of saved sessions are not hooked.
  event `{ agent: string; workspaceId: string | null; workspaceKind: "worktree" | "folder" | null; terminalId?: string; command: string; env: Record<string, string> }`; `next` may change `command`, `env`; stop with `{ deny: string }`
- `agent.prompt.before` (since 1.4.248): Orca is about to submit a prompt to an agent in a terminal: a launch prompt, an orchestration dispatch, an issue or task prompt, or a prompt sent with `orca terminal send`. A prompt a person submits is never hooked, and writes to one terminal stay in order while it decides. Rewrite `prompt` with `next`, or return `{ deny }` to refuse it.
  event `{ agent: string | null; terminalId: string; prompt: string; inputKind: "driving" | "orchestration" | "launch" }`; `next` may change `prompt`; stop with `{ deny: string }`
- `agent.tool.before` (since 1.4.248): An agent in an Orca terminal is about to run a tool. Claude Code waits for the answer: return `{ deny }` to refuse the call (the agent sees the reason) or change `input` with `next`; the person is still asked as usual. Other agents only report the call, so their results are ignored. Agents on SSH or WSL hosts are not hooked yet.
  event `{ agent: string; workspaceId: string | null; terminalId?: string; tool: string; input: JSON; callId?: string }`; `next` may change `input`; stop with `{ deny: string }`
- `agent.tool.after` (since 1.4.248): An agent in an Orca terminal finished a tool call (successfully or not). Observe only: Orca does not wait for it.
  event `{ agent: string; workspaceId: string | null; terminalId?: string; tool: string; input: JSON; callId?: string; output?: JSON }`; `next` may change nothing; stop with nothing (observe only)
- `editor.save.before` (since 1.4.248): The person is about to save a text file from an Orca editor tab (an explicit save, not autosave). Change `text` with `next` (format on save) or return `{ deny }` to refuse the save, which shows your reason. Edits made while the hook ran stay unsaved.
  event `{ workspaceId: string | null; path: string; languageId?: string; text: string }`; `next` may change `text`; stop with `{ deny: string }`

## Errors

A failed call rejects with an `Error` carrying `code`, `message`, `retryable` and, for `rate_limited`, `retryAfterMs`. Treat an unknown code as `action_failed`.

- `invalid_request`: the call itself is malformed
- `invalid_params`: params do not match the method, including a field this Orca does not know; the message names it
- `unknown_method`: the method does not exist in this Orca
- `capability_denied`: the manifest does not declare the capability
- `consent_required`: the plugin is disabled or the user has not approved this version
- `not_permitted`: the method or document is not available here, e.g. a worker-only method from a panel
- `rate_limited`: calls arrive faster than the budget; `retryAfterMs` says when to try again
- `unavailable`: the service behind the method is not running yet
- `action_failed`: the method ran and failed
- `cancelled`: the caller aborted the call through its `signal`
- `timeout`: Orca gave up waiting
- `conflict`: the call was made against a stale version, e.g. an editor edit after an outside change
- `too_large`: the message is larger than Orca accepts

# CI runners

Default to free GitHub-hosted standard runners: the repository is public and the
Enterprise plan allows 1,000 concurrent jobs (50 macOS). Use Blacksmith only for:

- macOS packaging: adhoc, hourly, daily and `release-mac-build.yml`. Hosted
  `macos-15` cannot boot the packaged x64 terminal host that `afterPack` verifies.
- The adhoc Windows build (a developer is waiting).
- Hardware-sensitive performance benchmarks. Operation-count contracts
  (`performance-contracts.yml`) are not, and run hosted.

PR checks run entirely on hosted runners. Unit tests
run as 12 shards on `ubuntu-24.04-arm`, which match the old five 8-vCPU
Blacksmith shards; `ORCA_UNIT_FULL_SHARD_COUNT` tunes the count. Preflight (lint
and typecheck) also runs on hosted ARM: shards, packaging and the layout oracle
do not wait for it, so its slower runner stays off the gate's critical path.
The layout oracle and advisory e2e lanes run on `ubuntu-24.04`. Git
compatibility runs one Git version per hosted job: three lanes sharing one
4-vCPU runner pushed real-Git tests past their timeouts.

Everything else, including the hourly and daily Windows builds, template
qualification and node-server lanes, runs on hosted `ubuntu-*`, `macos-15` and
`windows-2022` images. Do not use paid GitHub
larger runners: they cost more than Blacksmith at every size and Enterprise
included minutes do not cover them.

On Blacksmith, small routing and reporting jobs use 2 vCPUs; most test jobs use
4; compilation and shared JavaScript builds use 8. Mac checks use the 6-vCPU
Apple Silicon runners, including adhoc and release Mac packaging.

Keep matrix platform keys separate from runner labels: platform keys select
native slots, architectures, cache identities, and upload conditions.

## Cache stores

Blacksmith redirects `actions/cache` to its own store ("Enabling Blacksmith
transparent cache"); GitHub-hosted jobs use the repository's Actions cache. The
stores do not share entries, so the warmers (`ci-cache-warmup*.yml`) seed each
identity in both pools. Native module keys include the OS image, so a hosted
`ubuntu-22.04` consumer needs a hosted `ubuntu-22.04` warm leg.

GitHub's Actions cache is capped at 10 GB per repository and evicts the least
recently used entries first. Seed shared caches from `main`; avoid per-PR saves
of large or single-use artifacts, and prefer the lookup-only and restore-only
patterns in `.github/actions`.

## Production signing

SignPath requires every job in the signing workflow to use GitHub-hosted runners,
including jobs inside reusable workflows. `release-cut.yml` therefore explicitly
passes `fast_runners: false` to template qualification and `runner: ubuntu-latest`
to dependency security and shared JavaScript compilation. Preserve these overrides
when changing shared defaults.

The production Mac build already runs on Blacksmith in the separately dispatched
`release-mac-build.yml`. Keep its exact-run identity checks and publication gates.
Moving more production work to Blacksmith requires another isolated workflow;
changing a runner label inside `release-cut.yml` breaks signing provenance.

## Platform exceptions

These stay on GitHub-hosted runners even where the policy above picks Blacksmith:

- Windows WSL and WSL2 tests retain GitHub runners: Blacksmith Windows runners do
  not support the required nested virtualization.
- Windows signing and its rehearsal retain GitHub runners for SignPath provenance.
- Intel Mac and Windows ARM qualification retain their native GitHub runners;
  Blacksmith does not offer these architectures.
- Windows desktop lifecycle tests retain their existing GitHub desktop images.
- Mac SSH hostile-host tests retain GitHub images because Blacksmith's shell
  initialization restores the toolchain PATH that these fixtures must hide.
- Linux libc qualification keeps its pinned manylinux and Alpine containers,
  regardless of the host runner pool.

The shared dependency installer preserves temporary login-shell homes on
Blacksmith Linux hosts. Container jobs skip this host-image adjustment.

Runner availability: <https://docs.blacksmith.sh/blacksmith-runners/overview>.
Signing requirements: <https://docs.signpath.io/trusted-build-systems/github>.

# Unit test input ownership

Unit selection remains advisory. Every PR still executes the full unit inventory.

`config/scripts/ci/unit-selection/dependency-graph/ci-unit-input-ownership.json` records reviewed indirect repository inputs. A record covers the entire local source closure reachable from its `file`, including type imports. It does not remove ordinary import edges. Other callers of an indirect reader retain their own conservative fallback.

- `inputs`: exact repository paths or directory prefixes ending in `/`. Directory ownership includes new files. Unknown, deleted, renamed and global inputs still select the full suite.
- `emptyEnv`: optional external input overrides that must be absent or empty for the declaration to apply.
- `sourceClosureSha256`: `unitInputSourceDigest` of the sorted path/content entries in the local import closure. Unresolved or ambiguous package-directory imports cannot qualify.
- `contextSha256`: fingerprint of locked dependencies and the selection policy and unit runner/setup source closures. Dependency, policy or shared-runtime changes invalidate earlier review.
- `reason`: what was reviewed and why these inputs are sufficient.

The transcript replay record owns its captured-fixture directories and rejects optional external transcript/addon overrides. The compiler census owns all source, configuration and test directories. Reviewed URL/data projections have no indirect repository inputs.

A missing, malformed, duplicated or stale record keeps the conservative behavior. Before updating fingerprints, review the changed source closure, dependency/runtime context and any indirect reads again. Regenerating a digest does not establish ownership. The graph exposes `ownershipContextSha256`; source digests use `unitInputSourceDigest` from `ci-unit-input-ownership.mjs`.

For an eligible plan, `ci-shards/unit-selection.json` lists `checkedInputOwners`. Full successful and failing references, input addition/deletion/rename cases and hosted timing evidence are required before changing execution policy. Omitted worker time overlaps across processes and must not be reported as runner savings.

# Worktree storage maintenance

Run one command from the repository to preview maintenance across its locally registered Git worktrees:

```sh
pnpm reclaim-space
```

In an interactive terminal, the preview offers `Apply this cleanup? [y/N]`; enter `Y` to apply it.
Redirected input or output remains preview-only. To apply without a prompt, use `pnpm reclaim-space --apply`.

Historical test checkouts inside a worktree are removed only when the worktree is idle for 7 days:
no running process references its path, HEAD has not moved, and no changed or untracked Git path
was modified. To include active worktrees too, stop cross-version tests in all this
repository's worktrees, then preview with:

```sh
pnpm reclaim-space --tests-stopped
```

Answer `Y` to apply that preview, or use `pnpm reclaim-space --apply --tests-stopped` to apply directly.

The command reuses the historical test cache, Electron distribution, dev bundle, and Vite cache cleanup scripts.
It shares complete Electron distributions through the repository cache and removes idle
`out/electron-dev` bundles, which development rebuilds on demand. It also removes tracked
`.cache/vite` dependency caches unused for 30 days. It also removes stamped historical test
checkouts and shared seeds older than 30 days; tests regenerate them when needed. It leaves source files,
worktree registrations and branches intact. Manual and automatic cleanup also include old dependency
installs and build output as described below. Reported sizes are
logical file data; APFS clones and hardlinks mean actual disk savings can be smaller.

Use `--release-cache-min-age-days 7` to shorten historical-cache retention, or `0` to select all
recognised completed historical checkouts. This age option applies only to test caches. Local
checkout age uses directory modification time, which ordinary reuse does not refresh. Shared seeds
are protected by the copy lease, so they need no flag. Older harnesses hold no lease while reading
a local checkout, so local checkouts are selected only from idle worktrees (as defined above;
ignored files such as agent tooling directories do not count, and an unreadable process table or
Git failure counts as active). `--tests-stopped` acknowledges stopped
tests and includes active worktrees; it does not detect running tests.
Cache cleanup skips symlinks, malformed stamps, future formats, and publication/copy locks.
See [release source sharing](./release-source-sharing.md) for the cache and locking details.

Vite dev servers record cache use at startup and shutdown. Cleanup retains recent caches,
caches owned by a live process, and caches whose ownership cannot be verified, including caches
created before tracking was added. A maintenance lock prevents cleanup racing with server startup.
Desktop and web caches are reclaimed together; the next dev launch regenerates them as needed.

Use `--repo DIRECTORY` to choose another local repository. Git's worktree list determines scope,
including registered worktrees outside Orca's workspace directory. Folder workspaces without Git
have no repository-wide sweep. These commands run on the local host: they do not inspect or delete
anything on SSH hosts. Run maintenance on the execution host when maintaining remote repositories.

## Old dependency installs and build output

Old generated files are included in the normal manual command and automatic dev cleanup:

```sh
pnpm reclaim-space
pnpm reclaim-space --apply
```

This pass retains the selected repository worktree, the invoking worktree, and any
`--exclude-worktree` directory. It removes ignored, completely untracked `node_modules`, `out`,
`dist`, and `build` directories older than 30 days. Recognized package roots are the repository
root, `mobile`, `native/*`, `src/packages/*`, `cloud/apps/*`, and `cloud/packages/*`, each with a
regular `package.json`. It does not search arbitrary folders or the user's home directory.
Use `--generated-min-age-days 14` to shorten retention, or `0` to include recent generated
directories. Age is the directory modification time, not proof that an install is unused.
Old sibling installs and output can be removed while sibling work is running; reinstall
dependencies or rebuild in that worktree if needed. Shared pnpm package data is retained.

Preview leaves files in place. Apply rechecks Git tracking, parent paths, directory identity
and modification time before deleting. Symlinked directories, symlinked package parents, nested
repositories and directories containing tracked files are retained. Read-only generated
directories can be made writable for removal; hardlinked package files are never chmodded.
Source files, local changes, worktree registrations, branches, and shared pnpm stores remain
intact. Generated files are recreated by installing dependencies or rebuilding in that worktree.
APFS clones and hardlinks mean directory sizes can greatly overstate the actual space reclaimed.

Machine-wide caches, Docker images/volumes, downloads and simulator data remain
outside this repository-scoped command.

## Keeping installs shared

Healthy Electron installs join the shared distribution cache during native dependency setup,
without waiting for an Electron upgrade. The manual command migrates older installs immediately.
Read-only Electron package directories are retained and reported as skipped. Cache publication
or copying failures are also reported as skipped rather than silently omitted.

`pnpm dev` and `pnpm dev-stable-name` start an automatic repository-wide cleanup worker for
Electron, Vite caches, old dependency installs and generated output, and per-worktree dev
profiles whose worktree was removed (a profile is kept while its app, runtime, or terminal daemon
is still running),
in the background after the dev process starts. It never prompts or waits before launching the app.
The worktree being launched is excluded from every pass except historical test caches, which use
the idle-worktree rule. Existing bundle checks protect
active sibling Electron bundles and recent unfinished bundles from the bundle-specific pass;
the generated-directory pass uses its 30-day age cutoff and filesystem/Git protections.
Background sweep output is suppressed; worker start or exit failures are reported without stopping dev. Set `ORCA_SKIP_DEV_STORAGE_RECLAIM=1` to opt out.
The worker finishes independently if the dev app exits, and each cleanup operation has a ten-minute limit.

Automatic invocations also run historical test cache cleanup with the idle-worktree rule; they
never pass `--tests-stopped`, so active worktrees keep their local checkouts.
The repository lock prevents competing cleanup commands. Dev bundle removal checks active
processes and recent unfinished builds, then rechecks eligibility immediately before deletion.
An unreadable process table prevents removal.

To retain older bundles during a manual sweep, run the underlying command with an age limit:

```sh
node config/scripts/worktree-storage/reclaim-dev-electron-bundles.mjs --min-age-days 7 --apply
```

That limit uses the bundle directory's modification time. The underlying command also accepts
`--exclude-worktree DIRECTORY` to protect an entire worktree. A missing exclusion path is an error;
filesystem aliases resolve to the same worktree. Neither option schedules cleanup.

# Computer-use task benchmark

Compares Orca's direct Linux AT-SPI and Windows UI Automation providers with
cua-driver 0.38.0. This does not measure the CLI, sidecar, model, or complete agent
workflows. It does not install cua-driver in Orca.

Run the `Computer-use task benchmark` GitHub Actions workflow on a branch. Native
input runs only on its disposable Windows runner or Linux Xvfb desktop. The runner
refuses to run on the developer's desktop. Keep `ORCA_BACKGROUND_LAUNCH=1`.

The first matrix covers GTK/WinForms and Electron fixtures. Editor applications,
Wayland, macOS and additional Windows control frameworks need separate coverage.
Do not generalize these results to every application on a platform.

## Measurement contract

- Baseline and candidate runtimes come from full commit SHAs, copied before the
  run. Artifacts include source hashes, cua executable hash/version, image,
  seed, complete trial plan, responses, snapshots and independent fixture states.
- Each individual trial launches a fresh target, sentinel and provider. Process
  groups on Linux and jobs on Windows contain children, including timed-out calls.
  The provider is terminated and reaped before the terminal oracle read. No retry
  follows an uncertain mutation.
- Reset carries a unique nonce bound to the fixture instance and PID. The fixture
  acknowledges after applying text, selection, logical focus, counters, combo,
  scroll and menu state. Sentinel foreground and stacking are independently checked.
- Invalid preparation executes no provider operation, is excluded from the scored
  denominator, and makes the run incomplete with nonzero exit status. A missing or
  ambiguous control after valid setup is a scored coverage failure.
- Strict selectors require a unique matching role and label. References are fresh
  before the task and after every step. There is no label-only or role-only fallback.
- Completion requires exact independent final state, including unchanged decoy text
  and exactly one click/submit. Submission handlers capture the submitted text;
  Increment handlers capture the selected color at click time. Submit tasks require
  the marker in the submission, and choose-and-click requires Blue at the click.
  Final text/color alone cannot prove those events carried the intended values.
  Raw text is never cleaned. API errors, missing final
  observations and observed interference remain separate from task completion.
- The observer starts before provider initialization and initial selector snapshot,
  and stays active through all steps, reads, shutdown and settling. No sentinel
  refocusing happens during measurement. Idle and deliberate-steal controls must pass.
- Complete tasks run without simulated user typing. Separate click and scroll probes
  type `q` into the sentinel. Event counters preserve evidence even if agent input
  selects or deletes text. Observations sample roughly every 4 ms; they cannot prove
  the absence of shorter focus/pointer/clipboard changes. X11 clipboard observations
  detect ownership changes, not all changes made by the same owner.
- Engine order rotates across rounds from a recorded seed. Use a multiple of three
  rounds for balanced positions. Default/background and explicitly requested
  foreground profiles are separate trials. Foreground can intentionally interfere.
- Comparable per-step time includes the action and an additional full no-screenshot
  observation for every provider. Raw action time is diagnostic because Orca already
  returns a snapshot with mutations. Task time includes provider startup, discovery
  and all action/read pairs. Medians include completed tasks only; failed-attempt
  durations and sample counts are separate. Diagnostic serialization and disk I/O
  happen after timing. Final independent readback after shutdown is an upper
  bound on effect time, recorded separately.
- Fatal errors, invalid setup, failed observers, unobserved completion, budget
  exhaustion or missing planned cells leave JSON evidence and exit nonzero. A valid
  observed task failure remains a benchmark result, not an infrastructure failure.

Tasks cover explicit text targeting with another field logically focused, Unicode
entry plus submit, select-all replacement plus submit, and color choice plus one
click. Interference probes remain separate from task latency comparisons.

Explicit-target typing is a native capability probe. Orca's public CLI/RPC accepts
an element target for text (`type-text --element-index`) on providers that report
`actions.typeTextElement` (macOS, Linux and Windows). Click-then-type tasks send no element with the text, like `type-text`
without the index, although this benchmark still bypasses public transports.

The Linux Electron job also records restoration stages in `focus-probe/results.json`.
It records the AT-SPI focus acknowledgment, selected ACTIVE state, manual legacy PID
fallback, managed/native IDs, explicit singleton activation, minimized restoration
and the candidate's behavior with two same-PID windows. Managed windows include
minimized windows and exclude unmanaged helper windows.
The primary fixture publishes its native ID, checked against its PID before the probe.
Probe success establishes restoration behavior; actual text-and-submit completion
comes from the separate task results above.

AT-SPI ACTIVE is the runtime's focus authority. Global input can still race a later
focus change, and singleton accessibility/native counts do not establish an atomic
identity mapping if a window closes or the accessibility tree is stale. The probe
covers stable fixtures and detected ambiguity, not those concurrent lifecycle races.

Transports, fixtures and observers were adapted from the historical
`bench/computer-cua` prototype at `68a68ccf0f16c0a7f952d55adfe21850247b8ee9`.
Historical checkouts and result artifacts remain unchanged.

# Native chat tool pairing

Latest follow-up: [mobile row identity](./mobile-row-identity.md) keeps an opened detail with its command after earlier rows disappear or move.

Long tool runs repeatedly scanned all unanswered calls to find each named result.
Calls that emitted no output stayed at the front of that scan. Positional results
also shifted the remaining pending-call array after every answer.

The shared matcher now uses a linked FIFO and builds an ID index only when a
named answer needs to match beyond its head. That index stays valid until the
pending queue empties. Named and unnamed answers remove a pending call without
array movement; each call enters the index at most once. Duplicate IDs retain
FIFO order. Existing pair limits and output references are preserved.
The implementation remains shared by desktop, mobile, and host readers.

The rendered check exposed related correctness defects: Claude and Codex
transcript decoders discarded result IDs, and folding used only call counts to
assign results. Decoders now retain the optional provider ID; folding uses
the canonical matcher and occurrence indices, so an unrelated result cannot
consume another call's answer. Unmatched named results stay visible separately
and cannot acquire a guessed owner during later folds. Results without IDs
remain positional; already imported calls missing IDs cannot own named results.

Legacy journal import also preserves IDs on singleton calls and keeps singleton
results as result messages. The focused importer/projector regression test
covers reverse batched results, mixed record shapes, duplicate IDs, anonymous
FIFO, and old persisted calls whose IDs were already lost. That integration
coverage is separate from the rendered transcript fixture below.

# Hello Worker Panel

A components panel written in TSX with no build step, and the plugin's own worker. Start from
[hello-tsx](../hello-tsx) for a panel alone; this one adds everything a panel can reach beyond its
own UI, so it runs as a full-access (`trusted-worker`) plugin. Orca transpiles `src/*.tsx` and
`src/*.ts` when the panel loads (types stripped, JSX compiled for `orca`, relative imports such as
`./todos` resolved to their files).

```sh
orca plugin dev load .   # also writes .orca/types, the typings tsconfig.json extends
npx tsc -p .             # optional type check
```

Import only `orca` and relative files: there is no bundler, so `import 'react'` fails with an
error naming the file and the import.

It shows one of each part of the API:

- **Components**: keyed atoms, `derived` values, `setup(ctx)` and `ui.has` feature detection.
- **Panel → worker**: Suggest calls `plugin.request('tasks.suggest')`, answered by
  `orca.panels.handle` in `worker/main.mjs`, which starts on the panel's first request.
- **Worker → panel**: the worker `orca.panels.post`s `tasks.allDone` when the last task is done;
  the panel hears it with `plugin.on`.
- **Shared storage**: the task list is `atom('todos', ..., { persist: 'storage' })`, so the
  worker reads the same value with `orca.storage.get('todos')` and hears each change.
- **Settings**: `contributes.settings` declares `celebrate`, `suggestions` and `suggestionOrder` (a switch, a text box and a picker); change them under
  the plugin in Orca's Settings and the worker reads them with `orca.settings.get`.
- **Events**: `on('agent.status.changed')` counts working agents (the `agent:read` capability).
- **One typed contract**: `src/protocol.ts` declares `PluginRequests` and `PluginPanelEvents` in
  `declare module 'orca'`, so both sides type-check against it.

title: Race three agents on the same task
---

Running the same task across multiple agents in parallel is Orca's killer move. Same prompt, three branches, pick the winner.

## Steps

1. Create three worktrees from the same start-from ref. Name them `fix-bug`, `fix-bug-2`, `fix-bug-3`.
1. Launch a different agent in each — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor CLI.
1. Paste the same prompt into all three.
1. Watch the sidebar [status indicators](/docs/model/agents-sessions#state-indicators) and jump between worktrees with `Cmd-J` (macOS) / `Ctrl-Shift-J` (Windows / Linux) — each worktree keeps its own pane layout.
1. When they finish, review each diff. Use [Annotate AI Diff](/docs/review/annotate-ai-diff) on the winner.
1. Commit, push, open PR from the winning worktree.
1. Delete the two losers — one click removes the worktree and branch.

## Why it works

Different agents make different mistakes. Running the same task in parallel is cheaper than sequential retries and surfaces disagreement as a signal. Where three agents agree, the answer is probably right. Where they split, you've found the hard part.
